When interpreted in the type theory for higher-order classical theory this diagram tells us that
W
at the very least has type

W:(((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime}))\otimes((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime})))\rightarrow(I\rightarrow I).

To be a Boxworld process tensor we need
W
to be normalised on any Boxworld instrument as defined in
[
6
]
meaning that it must be normalised on any map of type
(A\rightarrow A^{\prime})\rightarrow((B\otimes X)\rightarrow(B^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime}))
. To prove the relevant type embedding, we use the BV logic of higher-order causal categories
[
59
]
, as well as a few specific features of higher-order causal categories (HOCCs).
First, in any HOCC we have that

\displaystyle(A\rightarrow A^{\prime})\rightarrow((B\otimes X)\rightarrow(B^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime}))

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle(B\otimes X\rightarrow A)\olessthan(A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime})

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle((B\rightarrow A)\invamp(X\rightarrow I))\olessthan((A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime})\invamp(I\rightarrow X^{\prime}))

then in any BV-category we have the following embedding

\displaystyle((B\rightarrow A)\invamp(X\rightarrow I))\olessthan((A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime})\invamp(I\rightarrow X^{\prime}))

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow

\displaystyle((B\rightarrow A)\olessthan(A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime}))\invamp((X\rightarrow I)\olessthan(I\rightarrow X^{\prime}))

and finally again using the causal decomposition property of HOCCs:

\displaystyle((B\rightarrow A)\olessthan(A^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime}))\invamp((X\rightarrow I)\olessthan(I\rightarrow X^{\prime}))

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle((A\rightarrow A^{\prime})\rightarrow(B\rightarrow B^{\prime}))\invamp(X\rightarrow X^{\prime}).

Let us now use this embedding on the following type:

\displaystyle((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow((B_{1}\otimes X_{1})\rightarrow(B_{1}^{\prime}\otimes X_{1}^{\prime})))\otimes((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow((B_{2}\otimes X_{2})\rightarrow(B_{2}^{\prime}\otimes X_{2}^{\prime})))

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow

\displaystyle(((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime}))\invamp(X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime}))\otimes(((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime}))\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime}))

then we proceed by using the symmetry isomorphism and distributors of BV-categories

\displaystyle(((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime}))\invamp(X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime}))\otimes(((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime}))\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime}))

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle((X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime})\invamp((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime})))\otimes(((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime}))\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime}))

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow

\displaystyle(X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime})\invamp(((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime}))\otimes(((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime}))\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime})))

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow

\displaystyle(X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime})\invamp(((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime}))\otimes((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime})))\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime})

Finally, we can simply apply
W:(((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime}))\otimes((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime})))\rightarrow(I\rightarrow I)
, in tensor product with two identity transformations as follows

\displaystyle 1_{X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime}}\invamp W\invamp 1_{X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime}}:

\displaystyle(X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime})\invamp(((A_{1}\rightarrow A_{1}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{1}\rightarrow B_{1}^{\prime}))\otimes((A_{2}\rightarrow A_{2}^{\prime})\rightarrow(B_{2}\rightarrow B_{2}^{\prime})))\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime})

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle(X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime})\invamp(I\rightarrow I)\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime})

to return the type

\displaystyle(X_{1}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime})\invamp(I\rightarrow I)\invamp(X_{2}\rightarrow X_{2}^{\prime})\cong(X_{1}\otimes X_{2}\rightarrow X_{1}^{\prime}\otimes X_{2}^{\prime}),

which is indeed the space of all bipartite probability distributions.

Indeed, by their types each
T_{i}
is by definition NS.
Furthermore in precisely this setup what remains after contracting with
W
is something which lies in the Boxworld tensor product of two parties, that is, a no-signalling channel. Consequently, any CJ-supermap on Boxworld satisfies no signalling without system exchange (NSWSE).

What remains is to prove the converse, that if a matrix in
\mathsf{Mat}_{\mathbb{R}^{+}}
is a NSWSE Boxworld tensor, then indeed that is sufficient to conclude that it is a CJ-supermap on Boxworld. First, let us consider a diagram of the following form,

The same reasoning process can be applied to each party, demonstrating that the induced state is multiparty non-signalling and so a state in Boxworld. This completes the proof.
∎

Appendix B
Proof of Lemma
1

In this section we will prove that whenever a component of one parameterised instrument is equal to a component of another parameterised instrument, then the application of a categorical supermap will preserve this equality.
Before we do so, we must confirm convex linearity of categorical supermaps.

Lemma 2
.

Every component of a one-input categorical supermap on a generalised theory is a convex linear function.

Appendix C
Strong Profunctors and the Yoneda Lemma

As explained in
[
34
]
the definition of categorical supermaps can be stated completely within the language of
strong profunctors
also known as Tambara modules
[
61
,
46
]
.
The utility of making this identification is that the main results of this paper can be derived almost immediately by abstract nonsense as instances of the Yoneda lemma.
Let us now give a brief outline of how this works.
Readers interested in further details from the point of view of supermaps can find them in
[
34
,
35
]
, from the point of view of monoidal context theory in
[
55
,
53
]
and from the point of view of profunctor optics as used in computer science in
[
18
,
51
]
.

Given a symmetric monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
, we have in many places in this article written expressions like
\mathcal{C}(A,B)
and
\mathcal{C}(A\otimes X,A^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime})
for the sets of maps
A\xrightarrow{}B
and
A\otimes X\xrightarrow{}A^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime}
respectively.
These objects are in fact instances profunctors: for example the family of sets
\{\mathcal{C}(A,B)\}_{A,B}
is closed under composition on either side by morphisms from
\mathcal{C}
.

Definition 11

(Profunctor)
.

A profunctor
P:\mathcal{C}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is a functor
P:\mathcal{C}^{\textrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\xrightarrow{}\mathsf{Set}
.

In the case of
\mathcal{C}(-,-):\mathcal{C}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
, we send each pair
(A,B)
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
to the set
\mathcal{C}(A,B)
of morphisms
A\xrightarrow{}B
in
\mathcal{C}
.
Then for a morphism
g:B\xrightarrow{}B^{\prime}
of
\mathcal{C}
, we send it to the function which simply acts by post-composing with
g
,

f\in\mathcal{C}(A,B)\mapsto gf\in\mathcal{C}(A,B^{\prime}),

and similarly by pre-composition for any morphism
h:A^{\prime}\xrightarrow{}A
.
This special profunctor
\mathcal{C}(-,-)
is known as the hom-profunctor and plays a rather special role in the theory.

The family of sets
\{\mathcal{C}(A\otimes X,A^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime})\}_{X,X^{\prime}}
is also a profunctor
\mathcal{C}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
in a similar way to the hom-profunctor, but just by composition along
X
and
X^{\prime}
.
Note that
A
and
A^{\prime}
are fixed here, this is because these objects are the input to the supermap we will eventually define.
It is
X
and
X^{\prime}
that vary, for these model the environment around
(A,A^{\prime})
.
We write this profunctor as
\mathcal{C}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes-)
.

The profunctors we have so far are, in fact, not only compatible with composition in
\mathcal{C}
but also with the tensor product of
\mathcal{C}
.
Such profunctors are known as
strong
.

Definition 12

(Strong Profunctor)
.

A profunctor
P:\mathcal{C}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
is strong if it equipped with a natural transformation
\zeta:\mathcal{C}(-,-)\times P(-,-)\xrightarrow{}P(-\otimes-,-\otimes-)
such that a number of coherence conditions hold making
\zeta
essentially associative and unital
[
61
,
46
]
.

A strength for a profunctor
P
gives a way of “tensoring” elements of
P
with morphisms of
\mathcal{C}
.
In the case of
\mathcal{C}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes-)
the strength is simply given by the tensor product of
\mathcal{C}
.

Strong profunctors assemble into a category
\mathsf{StProf}(\mathcal{C})
whose morphisms are the strong natural transformations – these are simply natural transformations that commute with the strengths.
It turns out that this property captures precisely commutation with combs so that it is possible to restate the definition of a categorical supermap as follows.

Definition 13

(Categorical Supermap)
.

A categorical supermap is a strong natural transformation,

S:\mathcal{C}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes-)\xrightarrow{}\mathcal{C}(B\otimes-,B^{\prime}\otimes-).

This can be extended to the multi-input case, and we refer the reader to
[
34
]
for the details of this.

In the case that we are working with a CPT, categorical supermaps simply become natural transformations on the deterministic part of the theory,

S:\mathcal{C}^{\mathbf{d}}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes-)\xrightarrow{}\mathcal{C}^{\mathbf{d}}(B\otimes-,B^{\prime}\otimes-),

where
\mathcal{C}^{\mathbf{d}}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes-):\mathcal{C}^{\mathbf{d}}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow\mathcal{C}^{\mathbf{d}}
so that we only require
S
to commute with deterministic combs.

One of the main results about strong profunctors is their representation theory developed in
[
46
]
.
This result characterises strong profunctors as representations (copresheaves) of a certain category
\mathsf{Optic}(\mathcal{C})
of
coend optics
.
The reason for this name comes from their application to bidirectional data accessors
[
18
]
but the more quantum-inclined readers of this paper might be intrigued to learn that it bears close resemblance to combs.

Definition 14

(Coend Optics)
.

\mathsf{Optic}(\mathcal{C})
is the category whose objects
(A,A^{\prime})
are pairs of objects from
\mathcal{C}
and whose morphisms
(A,A^{\prime})\xrightarrow{}(B,B^{\prime})
are elements of the following set,

\int^{X}\mathcal{C}(B,X\otimes A)\times\mathcal{C}(X\otimes A^{\prime},B^{\prime}).

The integral symbol here is not actually an integral at all and is known as a
coend

[
43
]
.
The details of coends are not terribly important for this informal discussion, and one may effectively think of the earlier expression as an abstract way of describing the space of one-holed combs with input
(A,A^{\prime})
and output
(B,B^{\prime})
.

Remark 1
.

One may wonder why we do not just call this category
\mathsf{Comb}(\mathcal{C})
and this is because there is subtlety in the difference between coend optics and combs as envisaged in quantum theory.
The equivalence relation on the sets of combs and the set of coend optics depends on the underlying category
\mathcal{C}
and is not always the same.
See
[
33
,
34
]
for further discussion of this, but note that in the case that
\mathcal{C}
is compact closed, coend optics and combs coincide so there is no danger in making this correspondence.

We are now in a position to state the representation theorem.

Theorem 8

(
[
46
]
)
.

\mathsf{StProf}(\mathcal{C})\cong[\mathsf{Optic}(\mathcal{C}),\mathsf{Set}]
.

This is
the
theorem that allows us to reduce the proof of Theorem
4
to a couple of lines and justify its naming as the Yoneda lemma for compact closed categories.

Proof.

Note that

\displaystyle y_{(A^{\prime},A)}

\displaystyle=\int^{X}\mathcal{C}(-,X\otimes A^{\prime})\times\mathcal{C}(X\otimes A,-)\cong\int^{X}\mathcal{C}(-,X\otimes A^{\prime})\times\mathcal{C}(X,A^{*}\otimes-)

\displaystyle\cong\mathcal{C}(-,A^{*}\otimes A^{\prime}\otimes-)\cong\mathcal{C}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes-)

so that
\mathcal{C}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes\mathord{=})
is representable.
The result now follows immediately by the Yoneda lemma.

\displaystyle\mathrm{Nat}\big(\mathcal{C}(A\otimes-,A^{\prime}\otimes\mathord{=}),\mathcal{C}(B\otimes-,B^{\prime}\otimes\mathord{=})\big)

\displaystyle\cong\mathrm{Nat}\big(y_{(A^{\prime},A)},\mathcal{C}(B\otimes-,B^{\prime}\otimes\mathord{=})\big)

\displaystyle\cong\mathcal{C}(B\otimes A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\otimes A)

∎

The element in
\mathcal{C}(B\otimes A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\otimes A)
that is equivalent to the original supermap is given in the original proof by the action of
S
on the swap.
The Yoneda lemma is precisely the reason that this appears.
